One-page synthesis

Verdict: Read soon. A comparatively strong prospective, paired, multicenter evaluation showing that technician-reviewed AI preclassification can improve analytical agreement and substantially reduce smear-review time. The evidence supports local workflow evaluation—not autonomous clinical deployment or claims of improved patient outcomes.

Core thesis

When junior-to-mid-level morphology technicians reviewed and corrected AI-generated cell classifications, the resulting workflow generally agreed more closely with expert-adjudicated morphology references than conventional manual review by the same technician. The largest operational effect was a reduction in median total review time from 852 to 328 seconds per smear.

What is most convincing

The paired design controls inter-sample variation; reading order was randomized; readings were separated by at least two weeks; technicians were blinded; expert adjudication was used for morphology; and flow cytometry served as the platelet reference. The study evaluated nucleated cells, 13 red-cell morphologies, platelet estimation, and time rather than restricting validation to white-cell preclassification.

What is not established

The study did not test clinical management, turnaround-to-treatment, bleeding, transfusion outcomes, diagnostic delay, or patient safety. It used one vendor platform, one smear-preparation system, standardized staining, and hematology-enriched tertiary centers. Rare-cell estimates were imprecise, supplementary analyses and code were unavailable in the supplied material, and the disease-screening analyses should be interpreted as alert-performance examples rather than independent diagnostic validation.

Study question and design

PopulationResidual EDTA-anticoagulated samples meeting International Consensus Group smear-review rules or clinician-requested review. Of 1,574 screened samples, 1,570 were analyzed; 99.8% required manual review.
Intervention / index workflowMC-100i scanning and AI preclassification or pregrading, followed by technician review and correction.
ComparatorConventional manual microscopy by the same technician on the same smear, after a washout period and in randomized reading order.
Reference standardsTwo senior experts with third-reader adjudication for nucleated and red-cell morphology; CD41/CD61 flow cytometry for platelet estimates; clinical diagnosis for APL and myelofibrosis screening analyses.
Primary endpointsNucleated-cell pass-rate superiority; RBC morphology accuracy non-inferiority (margin −5%); platelet agreement with flow cytometry.
Secondary / application endpointsReview time; APL and myelofibrosis screening; platelet threshold classification at 20 and 50 ×10⁹/L.

Section-by-section condensation

Abstract

The authors report a prospective multicenter evaluation of AI-assisted peripheral blood morphology using 1,570 smears. The abstract emphasizes improved performance across nucleated-cell and most erythrocyte categories, more accurate platelet estimation, improved APL and myelofibrosis-related morphology screening, and an approximately 60% efficiency gain.

The abstract correctly reflects the analytical and workflow findings but compresses several limits: rare positive counts, device-specific conditions, wide platelet limits of agreement, low myelofibrosis F1 score, and absence of clinical outcome testing.

Introduction

The rationale is that manual morphology is resource-intensive, operator-dependent, difficult to standardize, and challenging to archive or share. Digital morphology analyzers can preclassify cells using deep neural networks, but prior evidence has largely been retrospective, single-center, limited to white-cell classification, or focused on instrument-level concordance rather than incremental operator benefit.

The stated gap is clinically relevant: whether AI assistance helps routine technicians produce results closer to expert references across nucleated cells, red-cell morphologies, and platelet estimates while reducing review time. The intended contribution is regulatory-grade workflow evidence for the MC-100i.

Methods

Fresh residual samples were collected at three centers from March through October 2023. Three standardized Wright–Giemsa smears were prepared per sample. Smear A supported both paired workflows; smears A–C supported expert references. Samples were randomized 1:1 to AI-first or manual-first sequences with at least a 14-day washout. Technicians and experts were blinded to relevant prior results.

The AI workflow used human verification rather than autonomous output. Nucleated-cell evaluation targeted 200 cells, with lower minimums for leukopenia. RBC morphology used ordinal grades converted to binary positivity thresholds. Platelets were estimated from image-derived platelet/RBC counts and LIS RBC concentration, with flow cytometry as reference. Statistical methods included fixed-effect risk differences, a −5% RBC non-inferiority margin, Passing–Bablok regression, Bland–Altman analysis, CCC, Spearman correlation, and confusion matrices.

Results: cohort and baseline

Four Center 2 samples were excluded, leaving 656, 306, and 612 samples at Centers 1, 2, and 3. Centers differed in age, blood counts, diagnosis mix, and clinician-requested review rates; sex distribution did not differ significantly. The cohort was highly enriched for samples already requiring manual review.

This enrichment is appropriate for testing smear-review workflow performance but limits inference to unselected routine CBC populations. Center heterogeneity broadens case mix, while standardized equipment and protocols narrow technical diversity.

Results: nucleated-cell classification

AI assistance favored manual microscopy across the reported cell categories. The largest pooled pass-rate gains were lymphocytes (+10.79 percentage points, 95% CI 8.55–13.03) and band neutrophils (+10.64, 95% CI 8.00–13.27). Agreement gains were marked for difficult or clinically important categories: blast CCC 0.992 vs 0.945, abnormal promyelocyte CCC 0.991 vs 0.971, and plasma-cell CCC 0.763 vs 0.438.

The manuscript is internally inconsistent about formal superiority for three rare categories: one passage excludes plasma cells, abnormal lymphoid cells, and abnormal promyelocytes from significant superiority, while a subsequent passage states that their confidence limits met the superiority threshold. Rare positive counts and the sampling-error pass criterion constrain interpretation.

Results: red-cell morphology

Across 13 morphologies, AI assistance generally increased sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, and Youden index. Eight categories had risk-difference confidence intervals entirely above zero; the remaining five met the prespecified −5% non-inferiority criterion. Schistocyte sensitivity increased from 82.74% to 89.88%; teardrop-cell accuracy increased from 94.59% to 96.75%; basophilic-stippling sensitivity increased from 73.33% to 93.33%, though only 0.96% of samples were positive.

Polychromasia accuracy was slightly lower with AI (95.67% vs 96.50%), and rare morphologies have wide uncertainty. The system evaluates single-cell features but not smear-level arrangements such as rouleaux or agglutination.

Results: platelet estimation and thresholds

AI-assisted platelet estimates correlated more strongly with flow cytometry than manual estimates (Spearman 0.978 vs 0.948) and had lower mean bias (+2.05 vs −14.08 ×10⁹/L). The AI limits of agreement (−73.94 to 78.03) were narrower than manual limits (−123.16 to 95.00), but remain broad relative to low-count clinical thresholds.

At the 20 ×10⁹/L threshold, AI improved sensitivity (80.2% vs 70.9%), specificity (97.7% vs 95.9%), and accuracy (96.7% vs 94.5%). At 50 ×10⁹/L, sensitivity was similar/slightly lower (89.8% vs 90.9%), while specificity was higher (96.1% vs 94.5%). These results support decision-support use but not unqualified replacement of reference or confirmatory counting near thresholds.

Results: disease screening

Among 25 molecularly confirmed APL cases, AI-assisted review detected all 25, while manual microscopy missed one atypical case. AI specificity was 99.2% vs 98.4%, PPV 65.8% vs 50.0%, and F1 0.794 vs 0.658. This is clinically notable but based on a small positive sample and morphology-triggered screening, not a prospective management trial.

For myelofibrosis screening using teardrop cells ≥2+, AI sensitivity was 70.5% vs 62.3%, specificity 88.3% vs 87.3%, and F1 0.306 vs 0.261. The low F1 score underscores that teardrop-cell morphology is an imperfect screening proxy and should not be presented as a stand-alone diagnostic test.

Results: efficiency

Median total time fell from 852 seconds with manual microscopy to 328 seconds with AI assistance, a reported 61.5% reduction. The largest gain occurred in nucleated-cell classification, which fell from nearly 10 minutes of manual inspection to approximately 1.5 minutes of AI-assisted review.

The study measures analytical workflow time under its configured process; it does not provide cost-effectiveness, staffing, uptime, maintenance, failed-scan, rescanning, or full laboratory turnaround-time analyses.

Discussion, limitations, and conclusion

The authors interpret the findings as evidence that AI-assisted morphology can standardize review, improve consistency, support disease-related alerts, and enable traceable digital workflows. They appropriately state that patient-management and outcome effects remain untested.

Major limitations include rare categories, no comprehensive expert-validated cell-level error analysis, inability to detect malaria or smear-level RBC arrangements, standardized equipment and staining at all centers, restricted data access, unavailable supplied supplement, and sponsor/device dependence. The conclusion is reasonable when confined to structured decision support with professional review.

Purpose: Compare center-specific and pooled pass-rate risk differences for 15 nucleated-cell categories.
Main pattern: Pooled estimates favor AI assistance; largest gains were lymphocytes and band neutrophils.

Figure 3 — RBC morphology grading forest plots

Purpose: Compare accuracy risk differences for 13 RBC morphologies across centers.
Decision boundary: Dashed line = no difference; solid red line = −5% non-inferiority margin.
Main pattern: Eight categories were statistically superior; the remaining categories met non-inferiority.
Limit: Binary accuracy can obscure severity-grade disagreement; supplement-only confusion matrices were unavailable.

Workflow — Paired human-in-the-loop comparison

INPUT
  Residual sample meeting smear-review criteria
    ↓
STANDARDIZED PREPARATION
  Three Wright–Giemsa smears (A, B, C)
    ↓
RANDOMIZED READING ORDER
  AI-assisted → ≥14-day washout → manual
  OR manual → ≥14-day washout → AI-assisted
    ↓
AI-ASSISTED OUTPUT
  Device preclassification / pregrading → technician verifies and corrects
    ↓
MANUAL OUTPUT
  Same technician performs conventional microscopy
    ↓
REFERENCE
  Two senior experts; third expert adjudicates disagreement
  Platelet reference: repeated CD41/CD61 flow cytometry
    ↓
PAIRED PERFORMANCE AND TIME COMPARISON

Decision rule — Nucleated-cell pass criterion

A method result was classified as a “pass” when it fell within:

  expert reference proportion ± 1.96 × prespecified sampling standard error

The framework accounts for finite cell-count sampling error. It may be less sensitive to clinically consequential relative errors in rare cells, a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

Calculation — Platelet reference

Flow cytometry estimated the RBC-to-platelet particle ratio using CD41/CD61 labeling.
The calculated platelet concentration combined this ratio with the impedance-channel RBC concentration.
Each flow-cytometry test was repeated three times and averaged.

Evaluation and appraisal

Relevance

8/10

Strong fit for clinical AI validation, human review, and laboratory workflow design.

Basis: Real paired workflow, multiple morphology tasks, time measurement.

Limit: Less directly relevant outside hematology laboratories.

Raise/lower: Higher with outcome and implementation studies; lower if final publication materially revises results.

Novelty

8/10

Extends beyond instrument concordance to operator-level benefit across WBC, RBC, platelet, and time domains.

Basis: Prospective multicenter paired design and broad task coverage.

Limit: Single commercial platform and sponsor-linked regulatory evaluation.

Raise/lower: Higher with independent head-to-head platforms; lower if similar unpublished regulatory studies already exist.

Method strength

8/10

Good internal design with random order, washout, blinding, paired samples, expert adjudication, and flow-cytometry reference.

Basis: Prespecified endpoints and uncertainty reporting.

Limit: Rare positives, no full cell-level adjudication, no multiplicity strategy reported, and unavailable supplement.

Raise/lower: Higher with complete protocol/supplement, independent replication, and adjudicated error taxonomy.

Evidence strength

7/10

Directly supports analytical agreement and efficiency claims, but not clinical-benefit claims.

Basis: Large paired sample and appropriate reference methods.

Limit: Surrogate analytical endpoints and small disease-positive groups.

Raise/lower: Higher with patient-management and outcome endpoints; lower if rare-category superiority does not survive final editorial correction.

External validity

6/10

Three centers and heterogeneous case mix help, but technical and institutional diversity is limited.

Basis: Multicenter tertiary cohort.

Limit: Same vendor device, slide maker, staining, and preprocessing; Chinese tertiary hematology enrichment.

Raise/lower: Higher with independent sites, varied equipment/stains, community labs, and other regions.

Implementation value

7/10

Useful template for local validation and human-in-the-loop deployment requirements.

Basis: Explicit workflow, reference construction, thresholds, and time components.

Limit: No cost, downtime, training burden, LIS integration validation, post-deployment monitoring, or safety outcomes.

Raise/lower: Higher with prospective deployment, economic analysis, and drift/override monitoring.

Critical strengths

  • Paired same-sample comparison minimizes biological variation between methods.
  • Randomized reading order and washout reduce order and recall bias.
  • Human verification is evaluated explicitly rather than conflating model output with final clinical output.
  • Reference standards are stronger than routine manual review alone.
  • Performance is category-specific and accompanied by confidence intervals.

Critical limitations and safety concerns

  • Analytical—not clinical—validation: no evidence that the workflow improves outcomes or management.
  • Rare-cell uncertainty: high-risk categories have small positive denominators and wide intervals.
  • Technical generalizability: all sites used identical preparation, staining, device, and preprocessing.
  • Residual platelet disagreement: limits of agreement remain wide near critical thresholds.
  • Disease-screening overreach risk: APL and MF analyses are morphology-triggered alerts, not stand-alone diagnosis.
  • Sponsor dependence: sponsor funded, supplied equipment, and coordinated centers; two authors were employees.
  • Reproducibility gap: restricted dataset and missing supplied supplement/code.
  • Source inconsistency: consent-waiver statement conflicts with exclusion for missing consent; rare-cell superiority wording is also inconsistent.
Do not use this paper to justify: autonomous sign-out, removal of expert escalation, cross-platform performance claims, or clinical treatment decisions based only on AI morphology output.

Implementation and practice translation

Use nowUse the study as a design template for local paired validation of AI-assisted morphology and as evidence that human review can preserve safety while reducing workload.
Do not change yetDo not replace confirmatory methods, expert escalation, or local threshold policies based on this study alone.
Local validation requirementValidate each cell category and platelet threshold under local smear preparation, staining, scanner settings, staff experience, and disease mix.
Operational controlsTrack overrides, false negatives, rescans, failed fields, rare-cell alerts, turnaround time, drift, and technician-specific disagreement.
Clinical alert designTreat APL-like abnormal promyelocytes, schistocytes, and teardrop-cell findings as escalation triggers with explicit confirmatory pathways.
Evidence needed nextIndependent cross-platform studies, enriched rare-cell cohorts, complete cell-level error analysis, cost-effectiveness, and patient-management outcomes.

Minimum safe deployment conditions inferred from the study

  1. Maintain technician verification and correction before report release.
  2. Define category-specific acceptance thresholds rather than relying on a single aggregate accuracy metric.
  3. Require expert review for rare or urgent morphologies and for discordant analyzer/manual findings.
  4. Use confirmatory counting near platelet transfusion thresholds when clinical consequences are high.
  5. Version and audit model software, staining/preparation parameters, and LIS integration.
  6. Monitor performance after deployment, especially after equipment, stain, workflow, or population changes.
Best use of the paper: a robust example of evaluating the incremental benefit of an AI-assisted human workflow rather than evaluating an algorithm in isolation.
